history.content: Why would Two ETFs tracking Identical Indexes Produce different Returns?

Even if two ETFs are tracking the same index, they can still produce different returns due to varying management fees and expenses. This is because these costs can eat into the returns of the ETF, causing a discrepancy in the total returns between two funds. However, from an investor's point of view, the nominal prices of the tracking funds are not important. What matters is that when the underlying index moves by a given percentage, the price of the tracking funds should also move by an equal percentage. Any small difference in total returns will be attributable to these management fees and expenses, which is why low fees are so important in passive investing.  Index fund and ETF returns are all publicly available so you don't have to guess.

While a typical expense ratio  for mutual funds is 1% (annualized real rate of return on the stock market - after inflation - is about 4%), ETFs like SPY (which reflects the S&P 500 index) have a much lower annual expense ratio, such as .09% or VOO, with its .05%.   Since there are both good and bad ETFs, buying only $1000 at a time the broker transaction fee will eat too much of your money. You want to keep such fees way down below 0.1%.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's role in monetary policy has three objectives: currency stability (primarily keeping inflation within a narrow band); full employment; and improved prosperity and welfare. Its primary weapon in this, is its setting of a target for the cash rate - the overnight money-market interest rate charged between financial intermediaries. Short-term market rates closely track this cash rate target, because the Reserve Bank controls the supply of funds that banks use to settle the transactions that use the overnight money-market interest rates. Australian capital markets are liquid, with many deposits / loans being on variable-rate or short-term rates; hence changes to the cash rate quickly propagate throughout the market. NB that the changes propagate, but not all interest rates are at the same level: the absolute values don't propagate. Different interest rates will reflect different loan periods, and different (perceptions of) risks. Banks are profit-maximisers.
